newsitem.title: FRANCE: Delors could be Jospin's foreign minister - paper.
newsitem.headline: Delors could be Jospin's foreign minister - paper.

text.p: Former European Commission president Jacques Delors could be France's foreign minister if the well-placed Socialist-led opposition wins Sunday's parliamentary election runoff, a newspaper said on Friday.

The left-wing Liberation daily, close to the Socialists, said Delors, a former Socialist finance minister in the 1980s, was favourite to take a superministry for foreign and European affairs if the left won.
There was no immediate comment from the Socialist party nor from Delors' office.

Liberation quoted no source for its report, but Delors, 71, has served as an elder statesman and moral supporter of Socialist leader Lionel Jospin during the campaign, giving his blessing to the party's conditions for joining a single European currency.
"(President) Jacques Chirac could hardly refuse him, and he would have the advantage of being able to talk on an equal footing with German chancellor Helmut Kohl," Liberation said.
Chirac, a conservative Gaullist, often criticised Delors' federalist approach to European integration before being elected in 1995 and has not consulted him since then.

Delors and Kohl are close friends and the former commission president is widely respected in Germany, where the prospect of an upset Socialist-Communist election victory has been viewed with some alarm.

Delors headed the Brussels-based European executive for a decade from 1985 until the end of 1994, presiding over the completion of the single European market and playing a major role in drafting the 1991 Maastricht treaty on economic and monetary union.

He was the left's favourite for the 1995 French presidential election but disappointed his supporters by announcing in December 1994 that he had decided not to stand, citing his age and the difficulty of governing with a right-wing parliamentary majority.
He has since concentrated his energy on founding a think-tank, Notre Europe (Our Europe), dedicated to research and policy proposals on European issues.

There has been no indication in recent months that he was contemplating a return to government office, but the Socialists' chances of winning the election were not regarded as likely until last Sunday's first round, in which the combined left comfortably outpolled the centre-right.
Liberation said the other possible contenders for the foreign ministry were centre-left ex-prime minister Michel Rocard, a member of the European parliament, and former premier Laurent Fabius.
